title: Moving Average from Data Stream
statement: Design a class that is constructed with a window size k and exposes next(val): it accepts one integer from an unbounded stream and returns the average of the last k values seen. If fewer than k values have arrived, return the average of all of them.
realWorld: Every metrics pipeline computes rolling statistics this way — mean request latency over the last 100 requests feeding an alerting rule, a moving average of CPU load driving an autoscaler, a smoothed bandwidth estimate in a congestion controller. The stream never ends, so retaining all of it is not an option; only the k values that can still leave the window matter.

examples.explanation: The first two answers average fewer than k values. On the fourth call the window is full, so 1 leaves as 5 arrives: (10 + 3 + 5) / 3 = 6.0.
k = 1, so every value immediately evicts the previous one and the average is just the latest value.
Negative values and a non-integer average. Returning an int here would report -1, which is the most common way this breaks.

bruteForce.idea: Append every value to a growing list. On each call, sum the last k entries of the list and divide.
code: private final List<Integer> all = new ArrayList<>();
for (int i = from; i < all.size(); i++) sum += all.get(i);
bruteForce.whySlow: Consecutive windows overlap in k-1 of their k values, and the loop re-adds every one of those. The previous call already computed a sum that differs from this one by exactly two numbers: the value that just arrived and the value that just expired. Re-adding the k-1 survivors is the waste — over m calls that is m*k additions to produce m answers that m*2 additions would have given. The list is the second waste: it grows without bound to hold values that can never re-enter the window.

patternIdentification: Two signals stack here. 'The last k things', with items entering at one end and expiring at the other in the order they arrived, is first-in-first-out — a queue, so that the expiring element is always identifiable in O(1). And when the quantity you report over a window is a sum (or a count), maintain it incrementally: add what enters, subtract what leaves, never recompute the middle. Together they are the fixed-size sliding window, and the general test for applying it is whether the window's answer can be repaired from the two elements that changed rather than rebuilt from all k.

optimized.idea: Hold the current window in a queue and the window's total in a running sum. Each call enqueues the new value and adds it to the sum; if that pushed the window over k, dequeue the oldest and subtract exactly that value. Divide by the queue's current size — not by k — so the warm-up calls, when fewer than k values have arrived, are correct without a special case.
code: private final Deque<Integer> window = new ArrayDeque<>();
private long sum = 0;   // long: 10^4 values of magnitude 10^5 would still fit in an int, but the habit is cheap
sum -= window.poll();   // subtract precisely what left; the k-1 survivors are never touched

commonMistakes: Dividing by `size` instead of `window.size()` — every answer before the window fills is wrong: with k = 3, next(1) returns 0.333 instead of 1.0. Tests that only inspect the steady state never catch it.

Integer division: keeping the sum in an int and writing `return sum / window.size();` returns 5 where 5.5 is correct, and -1 where -1.5 is correct. The values are plausible enough to pass a careless eyeball check.

Rebuilding the sum by iterating the queue after each eviction instead of subtracting the polled value — the answers are right, but next() is back to O(k) and the O(1) requirement quietly fails; on a 10^4-call stream with k = 1000 this is the difference between passing and timing out.
